The task asks for a rotation, so I kept the wraparound. The shared note says to use `n << d`, but a plain shift drops the high bits instead of moving them to the bottom. The two agree on your example, `left_rotate(16, 2)`, but not in general. For instance, rotating `0x80000000` left by 1 gives `1`, while a plain shift gives `0`.

```python
def left_rotate(x, d):
    """Rotate the 32-bit unsigned integer x left by d bits."""
    x &= 0xFFFFFFFF
    d %= 32
    return ((x << d) | (x >> (32 - d))) & 0xFFFFFFFF


assert left_rotate(16, 2) == 64
assert left_rotate(0x80000000, 1) == 1
assert left_rotate(0, 5) == 0
assert left_rotate(0x12345678, 0) == 0x12345678
```
